3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was what they had been warned to expect, and fearing that the tempter had talked them out of the faith. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding, and they long to see Paul as he longs to see them.

Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.” He cannot thank God enough, and prays night and day to see them and fill the gaps in their teaching. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will clear his road to them, make their love overflow to everyone, and strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness when Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Paul could stand it no longer, he chose to be left alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his brother and God’s co-worker, to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be unsettled by their troubles. They knew they were destined for this; Paul had told them in advance they would suffer, and so it happened. Unable to bear it, he sent to find out about their faith, afraid the tempter had tempted them and his work had been wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as Appointment, Not Accident

The key word in verse 3 is keimetha — we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the language of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted, and Paul uses the same root of himself in prison, put there for the defence of the gospel (Phil 1:16). Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God's attention; it is a placement.

That is the pastoral logic, and it needs stating carefully. What steadies a shaken believer is not the promise that the trouble will stop but the assurance that the trouble is not a mistake. If hardship means the plan has gone wrong, every difficult week is evidence against the faith. If hardship is where God has laid you, the difficult week proves only that you are where he put you. The Reformed tradition has held this consistently: God governs all things, his people's afflictions included, and such suffering is purposeful — producing endurance, character and hope (Rom 5:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v.3) — faith is usually lost by erosion, not by renunciation.

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and its absence is a cruelty disguised as encouragement (v.4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when we could stand it no longer, we decided to be left alone in Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s co-worker in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith.

Could bear it no longer. Stegō, to hold water out, as a roof or a watertight jar. Paul had been holding in his anxiety, and the seams gave way. He says it twice (vv. 1, 5).

Alone at Athens. The city where Paul was provoked by idols, mocked at the mention of resurrection, and made few converts (Acts 17:16–34): his thinnest ground. There, he gave away his companion. “Alone” stands last in the Greek, with weight. He chose isolation because a frightened church needed someone more than he did. That is 2:8, sharing “our own selves”, as an actual decision.

The sequence. Acts 17:14–15 has Silas and Timothy staying in Macedonia while Paul went on; they evidently rejoined him at Athens, then Timothy was sent back, and both met Paul again at Corinth (Acts 18:5).

God’s co-worker. Not “my assistant”. Steadying a church is God’s work, and Timothy works alongside God (1 Corinthians 3:9).

A textual note. Manuscripts vary: “God’s co-worker”, “minister of God”, or both combined. Scribes may have softened the bold “co-worker of God”. The ESV reading is probably original.

Establish and exhort. To prop a leaning wall, and to come alongside and urge. Under attack, the first task is not growth but keeping the church standing.

On a Tuesday. Whose need is greater than your comfort this week? Send help, even if it costs you company.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy came so that none of you would be shaken by these troubles. You know very well that we are destined for them.

Moved. Sainesthai, first used of a dog wagging its tail: fawned on, coaxed. Paul’s fear was not that persecution would smash them but that they would be gently talked out of the faith.

How faith is usually lost. Not by dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation easier to accept, the guild dinner too costly to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram (Mark 4:17).

Destined. Keimetha, “we are laid”: set in place like a foundation stone, posted like a sentry. The same root Paul uses of himself in prison: “I am put here for the defense of the gospel” (Philippians 1:16).

The pastoral logic. What steadies a shaken believer is not that the trouble will stop, but that it is not a mistake. If suffering means the plan has failed, every hard week is evidence against the faith. If it is where God has placed you, it proves only that you are where he put you (Romans 5:3–4; 1 Peter 4:12).

What it does not mean. Not that God delights in his people’s pain, or that we should seek suffering. Persecution is still evil; God rules it for good.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we were with you, we kept telling you that we would suffer persecution, and it turned out that way, as you know. That is why, when I could stand it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith. I was afraid that the tempter had tempted you and our work had been in vain.

Told beforehand. Continuous tense: he kept telling them, in a stay of a few weeks. He did not win them with an easier offer and explain the terms later (Acts 14:22).

Verified by events. When trouble came, it confirmed the teaching instead of contradicting it. A church told the truth can say “he said this would happen”; a church promised an easy road asks whether the whole thing was false.

The tempter. Satan’s title in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where the method was suggestion, not violence. Block the teacher (2:18), then work on the church.

In vain. Kenos, the “empty” of 2:1. The confident apostle also lay awake fearing his work had come to nothing.

Faith and anxiety. Paul was sure of God and frightened about the outcome at once. He could not go, so he sent, and waited (compare 2 Corinthians 11:28).

On a Tuesday. When you teach new believers, tell them honestly what following Christ costs. It is a kindness.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Timothy has returned with good news of their faith and love: they remember Paul fondly and long to see him, as he longs to see them. In all his own distress, their faith has comforted him. Now he truly lives, since they are standing firm in the Lord. He cannot thank God enough for the joy they bring, and prays night and day to see them and supply what is lacking in their faith. May God our Father and the Lord Jesus clear the way for him to come; may the Lord make their love for each other and for everyone grow and overflow, as his does for them; and may he strengthen their hearts to be blameless and holy before God when the Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Persons, One Verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb — the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man's prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v.10) was not sincerity but completeness — the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but ‘for all’ (v.12) — the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Timothy has just come back to us from you and brought good news about your faith and love. He tells us that you always have fond memories of us and long to see us, just as we long to see you. So, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and suffering we have been encouraged about you because of your faith.

The news arrives. The letter changes temperature.

Gospelled. Euangelisamenou, the verb for preaching the good news, used by Paul only here for anything other than the gospel. A church standing firm was good news of the same order.

Three fears answered. Faith: they had not been coaxed away. Love: they had not turned on one another. Remembrance: they had not concluded he abandoned them, as his enemies said.

The comforted apostle. Their faith comforts him. In Corinth he was “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10).

Two-way traffic. In a healthy church the strengtheners are held up by the ordinary believers they worry about (Romans 1:12).

On a Tuesday. If you wonder whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone: it was what got Paul through Corinth. Tell your pastor how you are doing.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we really live, since you are standing firm in the Lord.

Alive. Not merely relieved: alive. The months of not knowing were a kind of death.

What it does not mean. Not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on his people’s performance. Paul sought no glory from them (2:6). This is love, and love always makes your wellbeing hostage to someone else’s (3 John 4).

Standing fast. Stēkete, a soldier holding his place in the line (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). Not advancing or achieving; still there when the pushing stopped.

In the Lord. Not by stubbornness or loyalty to Paul. The place they held was a person.

On a Tuesday. These new converts had simply not given up. They did not know that their not giving up was what an apostle was living on. Neither do you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can we thank God enough for you, in return for all the joy we have in God’s presence because of you? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you again and supply what is lacking in your faith.

A real question. Paul has run out of ways to say thank you.

Before our God. Joy over others is held up in God’s presence, because he did it.

Most earnestly. A double superlative: the ordinary intensifiers would not carry it. “Night and day” is the phrase of 2:9: whatever Paul did at night, he did not sleep much.

What is lacking. Not a rebuke after eight verses of praise. Katartisai means to set a bone or mend a net (Matthew 4:21): to make complete. What was lacking was the teaching he never got to give in a few weeks. Chapters 4–5 begin to supply it.

Two kinds of gap. A deficiency that is a fault, and one that is an unfinished education. Paul meets the second not with reproach but with longing to fill it.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels patchy, ask whether nobody ever taught you. Then find a good teacher or book, and fill the gap.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you.

Two persons, one verb. The Father and the Lord Jesus are the subjects; the verb “direct” is singular. Paul names two and speaks of them acting as one, without explanation (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:16–17). Within twenty years of the cross, this is the ordinary shape of his prayer.

Clear the road. Kateuthynai, to make straight: against 2:18, where Satan “cut into” it. The enemy truly obstructs; the Sovereign truly governs; only one is prayed to.

Refused, for a while. So far as we know, Paul did not return for years (perhaps Acts 20:1–2). Instead came Timothy’s report and this letter, which has done more for the church than the visit could.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts add “Christ” after “Jesus”.

On a Tuesday. Pray about the blocked road, then do the work you can from where you are.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the Lord make your love for one another and for everyone else increase and overflow, just as ours does for you. May he strengthen your hearts so that you will be blameless and holy in the presence of our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

A flood. “Increase and abound”: multiply and overflow the banks.

And for all. The sharp phrase. A persecuted community naturally turns inward and keeps its warmth for insiders; that is the beginning of a sect. Paul prays they will overflow with love for the very people making their life hard (Matthew 5:44).

As we do for you. Paul’s love, demonstrated in chapters 2–3, is the measure.

The Lord makes you. Not “try harder”. Ask God for what you then work at (4:9–10).

Establish. What Timothy was sent to do (v. 2), Paul now asks God to do. That is how ministry works.

Blameless in holiness. The hinge into chapter 4, which begins with holiness (4:3).

With all his saints. Most likely the angels, on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5: “the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.” Others include believers who have died (4:14). Either way, a prophet’s picture of God arriving is applied to Jesus.

A textual note. Some manuscripts end the verse with “Amen”.

For worship. Love now is how a church gets ready for then.

parallels.desc: the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone,<sup>2</sup>and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,<sup>3</sup>that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.<sup>4</sup>For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know.<sup>5</sup>For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.<sup>6</sup>But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—<sup>7</sup>for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.<sup>8</sup>For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God,<sup>10</sup>as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?<sup>11</sup>Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,<sup>12</sup>and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you,<sup>13</sup>so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

4.title: Holy Living and the Blessed Hope
4.overview:
Paul now fills in what he could not teach in a few weeks. First, holiness: God’s will is that they be sanctified, above all by abstaining from sexual immorality, in a city where sex outside marriage was socially normal for men. Sexual sin wrongs a brother or sister, the Lord avenges it, and to reject this teaching is to reject God, who gives his Holy Spirit. Second, love and work: they are already “taught by God” to love one another, and should do so more and more, living quietly, minding their own business and working with their hands, perhaps because some had stopped working while waiting for Christ.

Third, the question that had shaken them: what happens to believers who die before Jesus returns? They are not lost. Christians grieve, but not without hope. Because Jesus died and rose, God will bring the dead with him. At his loud and public coming, the dead in Christ will rise first; then the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord, as citizens go out to welcome a king, and so we will always be with the Lord. Comfort one another with these words.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–8 – The Will of God Is Your Sanctification
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally, Paul asks and urges them in the Lord Jesus to live in a way that pleases God, as they are already doing, more and more, following the instructions he gave by the Lord’s authority. God’s will is their holiness: that they avoid sexual immorality; that each learn to control his own body in a holy and honourable way, not in passionate lust like those who do not know God; and that no one wrong or take advantage of a brother or sister in this, for the Lord punishes all such sins, as Paul had warned. God called them not to impurity but to holiness. Whoever rejects this rejects not a human being but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body, and Who Lives In It

Paul grounds Christian sexual ethics not in his own authority or in respectability but in the Holy Spirit, whom God goes on giving into the believer (v.8). The claim on the Christian's body is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in (cf. 1 Cor 6:19-20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property; Paul brought a different account of what a person is, and applied one standard to men and women alike.

Now: Verse 6 names the victim: sexual sin is always something done to a person, and the Lord is an avenger for those who never had redress.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers and sisters, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus: you learned from us how to live in order to please God, as in fact you are living. Now do this more and more. You know the instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus.

Finally. Not the end (two chapters remain), but the turn from report to request. What follows spells out the prayer of 3:13.

Ask and urge. A request and an appeal, not a command, from a man who could command (2:6).

To please God. Not a rulebook but a Person. You can satisfy a rule without thinking of its giver; you cannot please someone without thinking of him (2 Corinthians 5:9).

As you are doing. He confirms they are on the road before asking for more. Encouragement grows from what is good, not from a deficit.

More and more. Twice in this chapter (vv. 1, 10). No plateau at which growth becomes optional (Philippians 3:12–14).

Instructions. Parangelias, orders passed down a chain of command. These were never Paul’s; they came through him from Jesus, and he was under them too.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts lack “just as you are doing” (KJV). The earliest have it, and it fits Paul’s warmth.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is God’s will that you should be holy: that you keep away from sexual immorality; that each of you learn to control your own body in a way that is holy and honourable, not in passionate lust like the pagans, who do not know God.

The will of God. People long to know it. Paul states it in a sentence, and it is not about a job or a spouse: God intends to make you holy.

Sexual immorality. Porneia, every sexual act outside marriage.

The world it landed in. Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property. A married man’s use of slaves, prostitutes and concubines was socially normal; what was policed was another citizen’s wife, because that was theft. A speech preserved under Demosthenes’ name put it bluntly: courtesans for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives for legitimate children. Paul says the body is not property ruled by appetite, and one standard applies to men and women alike. Not a tightening of existing morality, but a different account of what a person is.

His own vessel. Skeuos means vessel. It may mean the body (ESV: self-control) or a wife (“take a wife for himself”, compare 1 Peter 3:7). The body is more likely, since the command is to “each one of you”, single and married. Either way the standard is holiness and honour, which forbids treating any person as an instrument of appetite.

Who do not know God. Not that pagans were uniquely wicked; some moralists taught restraint. When God is unknown, there is no reason to treat the body as more than a means of pleasure (Romans 1:24). The Christian difference is not superior willpower but knowledge of God.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes, remember: this is not about a rule but about what God is doing in you.
verseByVerse.note: To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself”; the phrase can be read either way.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this matter no one should wrong or take advantage of a brother or sister. The Lord will punish everyone who commits such sins, as we told you and warned you before.

The victim. Sexual sin is always done to someone. Pleonektein, from “to have more”: to overreach, defraud. A commercial word, because sexual sin takes what is not yours to get more for yourself.

Against “private matters”. There is always a person on the other side: the one used, the spouse betrayed, the family broken, the future spouse defrauded. Theft from someone Christ died for.

Avenger. Ekdikos: the one who brings justice for the wronged. Sexual sin often goes unpunished here, and the powerful keep their reputations. There is a court that does not work that way. For victims, this verse is a promise.

Warned beforehand. No new severity sprung on converts recruited on easier terms.

For the guilty. The God who avenges is the God who makes people holy (v. 3). “Such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). It is a warning precisely because there is a way out.

On a Tuesday. Before any choice about your body, ask: who would be wronged by this?

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God did not call us to be impure, but to live a holy life. So anyone who rejects this instruction rejects not a human being but God, who gives you his Holy Spirit.

The calling sets the character. Not an argument from health or social order, but from what they were summoned into. Holiness is not an optional extra; it is the content of the invitation (1 Peter 1:15–16).

Not man but God. Paul does not say “obey me, I am an apostle”. The instruction was never his (v. 2), so there is no one in between to argue with.

Gives his Spirit. Present tense: who keeps giving. And the preposition is “into you”.

Not moralism. The case for sexual holiness ends not with a threat but a Person living in the body under discussion: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit … You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The claim on your body is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “gave” and “to us”. The present “gives” and “to you” are better attested.

For worship. The Holy Spirit lives in you. Let that shape what you look at tonight.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:9–12 – Brotherly Love and the Quiet Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About brotherly love they need no instruction, for God himself has taught them to love one another, and they love all the believers throughout Macedonia. Still, Paul urges them to do so more and more, to make it their ambition to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands, as he told them, so that they will be respected by outsiders and not depend on anyone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Covenant, Landed

Theodidaktoi appears nowhere in Greek literature before this letter; Paul seems to have coined it. He is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah's new covenant promise — I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts, and they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest (Jer 31:33-34).

That is a considerable claim to make about a congregation of ex-pagans a few months old. Paul says the promised covenant has visibly arrived among them — and his evidence is not their doctrine but their love, which is the more striking because he was driven out before he could teach them much. What they know, God taught them from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Why would a church need telling to work? Almost certainly because of the subject of the next paragraph. If the Lord is returning imminently, why keep a trade, why plan, why save? The problem worsened rather than resolved: in the second letter Paul has to deal with people who are 'not busy at work, but busybodies', and rules that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thess 3:10-12). And 'work with your hands' was an affront to Greek sensibility — manual labour was for slaves and the poor, not for men with philosophical pretensions.

Now: The principle is one the letter keeps insisting on: expecting the Lord's return should make a Christian more reliable, not less. Idleness is treated here as a failure of love, because the idle man's food comes from somewhere and the somewhere is his brothers. Note too the ambition Paul actually commends — philotimeisthai hesychazein, make it your point of honour to be unremarkable. The New Testament's aim for most Christians is not a platform but ordinary competence: your own work done well, your own business minded, and nobody made poorer for having you around.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now about your love for one another we do not need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love each other. And in fact you do love all of God’s family throughout Macedonia. Yet we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more.

No need to write, but writing. A gracious way of raising a subject.

Taught by God. Theodidaktoi, found nowhere earlier in Greek: Paul seems to have coined it. He echoes the new covenant promise: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts … they shall all know me” (Jeremiah 31:33–34; compare Isaiah 54:13; John 6:45).

The evidence. Not their doctrine (he had little time to teach), but their love. What they know, God taught them from the inside.

Throughout Macedonia. Philippi, Berea, beyond. A poor, persecuted church reaching outside its walls: the answer to 3:12.

More and more. Name honestly what is good, then ask for growth from there.

On a Tuesday. Is your love limited to your own congregation? Help another church this month.

verseByVerse.quote: and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make it your ambition to lead a quiet life, to mind your own business and to work with your hands, just as we told you, so that your daily life may win the respect of outsiders and so that you will not be dependent on anybody.

Ambitious to be quiet. Philotimeisthai is the word for competing for public honour. Paul says: make it your ambition to be calm and unremarkable.

Mind your own affairs. Not everyone else’s (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

Work with your hands. An affront to Greek sensibility: manual labour was for slaves and the poor. Paul had done it among them night and day (2:9).

Why say it? Probably because of the next paragraph. If the Lord is coming soon, why keep a trade, plan or save? The problem got worse; in the second letter Paul rules that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

Hope makes you reliable. Expecting Christ should make a Christian more dependable, not less. Idleness is a failure of love: the idle man’s food comes from his brothers.

Before outsiders. An honest, working, calm church is an argument; a community of excitable freeloaders is an argument for the other side.

Dependent on no one. Not a rejection of generosity, but refusing to be a burden when you need not be.

On a Tuesday. The New Testament’s ambition for most Christians is not a platform but ordinary competence: work done well, bills paid, nobody poorer for having you around.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not want them to be uninformed about believers who have died, so that they will not grieve like those with no hope. Since Jesus died and rose, God will bring with Jesus those who have died in him. By the Lord’s word, the living will not go ahead of the dead. The Lord himself will come down from heaven with a loud command, the archangel’s voice and God’s trumpet, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then the living will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. So encourage one another with these words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Meeting on the Road

‘To meet the Lord’ (v.17) is the language of a city's delegation going out along the road to greet an arriving king and escort him in (cf. Acts 28:15). The passage gives one loud, public, personal arrival at which the Christian dead are raised first; it gives no timetable, and it settles less of the wider debate about the order of the last things than is often claimed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Against the bleak tomb inscriptions of that world, a Christian funeral in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else altogether.

Now: Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope (v.13); and the passage is for comforting one another at gravesides (v.18), not for building charts.

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who have died, so that you will not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope.

The emergency. Some believers had died. Paul had taught them to wait for Jesus (1:10), but not, in a few weeks, what happens to believers who die before he comes. Had they missed it?

Information for grief. Paul does not tell them to feel differently or pray harder. He tells them a fact, because their distress came from not knowing it. Sometimes the grieving need the truth more than more comfort.

Asleep. Koimaomai, the usual New Testament word for a believer’s death; our “cemetery” (sleeping-place) comes from it. Not that the soul is unconscious; Paul expects to “depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). It means death is temporary: there will be a waking.

Not like others. Paul does not forbid grief. Christians grieve; they do not grieve like people with nothing ahead.

What it does not mean. That tears are a failure of faith. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to open (John 11:35). Hope changes not whether you weep but what you know while weeping.

No hope. Accurate. Pagan epitaphs read: “I was not, I was, I am not, I care not.” A Christian funeral in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else entirely.

On a Tuesday. Sit with someone grieving, and do not rush them. When the time is right, tell them the truth of this chapter.
verseByVerse.note: “Asleep” was a common Christian way of speaking of believers who had died.

verseByVerse.quote: For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have died believing in him.

Resting on an event. The argument is one sentence, and it rests on history.

Union, not analogy. Not that Jesus’ resurrection makes resurrection seem plausible, but that believers are in him: what happened to the head happens to the body. “Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:23). The first sheaf is the harvest beginning.

Died, and asleep. Of Jesus, “died”: Paul will not soften Golgotha. Of believers, “asleep”. Because he took death whole, it has become sleep for his people.

Bring with him. The dead are not left behind; they come with Jesus. And they are with him now, which is why they can accompany him (2 Corinthians 5:8).

Through Jesus. The phrase can attach to “fallen asleep” or to “bring”. Either way, everything about a Christian’s death and future runs through one person.

For worship. Your believing dead are not at the back of the queue. They are in the King’s procession.

verseByVerse.quote: For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to the Lord’s own word, we tell you this: we who are still alive and remain until the Lord comes will certainly not go ahead of those who have died. For the Lord himself will come down from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first.

A word from the Lord. Revelation, not inference: a saying of Jesus not in the Gospels, or a direct disclosure. Paul is careful about this distinction (1 Corinthians 7:10, 12), so the flag can be trusted.

Modest and exact. Not a timetable, but one fact: the living will not get there first. There is no queue.

The Lord himself. Not an angel sent to fetch them. He comes in person (Acts 1:11).

Three sounds. Keleusma, an officer’s command; an archangel’s voice; God’s trumpet, which in Israel summoned the assembly and announced God at Sinai (Exodus 19:16; compare Matthew 24:31; 1 Corinthians 15:52). Public and loud. Nothing secret.

Is Jesus an archangel? Jehovah’s Witnesses identify him with Michael. No: he comes with an archangel’s voice, as with a trumpet. God never called an angel his Son, and all angels worship him (Hebrews 1:5–6).

The dead in Christ. Their union with him was never broken; death only interrupted what could be seen. Paul is answering one congregation about their own dead, not giving a full account of all resurrection (compare John 5:28–29).

Did Paul expect to be alive? “We who are alive” identifies him with whoever will be living then. He did not know when (5:1–2), and later expected to die (2 Timothy 4:6). He was not mistaken; he was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After that, we who are still alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord for ever.

Caught up. Harpagēsometha, seized, snatched (Acts 8:39). In Latin, rapiemur: hence “rapture”. The word is biblical; the question is what it describes.

To meet. Eis apantēsin, a near-technical term. When a ruler approached a city, citizens went out along the road to greet him and then escorted him back in. Luke uses it of the Roman Christians walking out to meet Paul and bring him to the city (Acts 28:15; compare Matthew 25:6).

The picture. Paul has used parousia, a royal visit (2:19). The King arrives; his people, the dead first and then the living, go out to meet him; and the procession comes home. Not the church removed from the earth, but the King coming to it.

A secret rapture? Pretribulational Christians hold that Christ first comes secretly to take the church, then returns visibly after a seven-year tribulation. But this coming is loud and public, and “meet” describes going out to escort an arriving king. The more likely reading is one public return, at which believers rise to meet the Lord and accompany him. Faithful Christians differ here; the passage gives no timetable (5:1–2).

In the clouds. Clouds in Scripture mark God’s presence (Exodus 19:9; Daniel 7:13; Acts 1:9).

Always with the Lord. Paul’s emphasis. Not “in the air”, which is merely where the meeting happens. The comfort is not the mechanism but the permanence. What they feared losing, Christ and each other, can never now be interrupted.

For worship. “Always” is the best word in the passage.
verseByVerse.note: “Meet” was the word used of citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him into the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another with these words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So encourage one another with these words.

What it is for. Not “construct a chart” or “divide from those who read it differently”. This was given to a bereaved church to use on each other.

A rebuke. These verses have generated libraries of speculation and heat between Christians who agree about the resurrection and Christ’s return. Measure our handling of them against the purpose Paul names.

One another. Not only leaders. Ordinary believers comforting each other with doctrine. That assumes they know each other’s griefs and know the teaching.

These words. The actual words, to be repeated at the graveside and to the widow weeks later when everyone else has gone back to normal.

Obeyed for two thousand years. One of the passages most read at Christian funerals.

On a Tuesday. Learn verses 13–18 well enough to say them to someone who is crying.

5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview:
After answering what happens to believers who die, Paul answers the next question, “When?”, by declining to give a date. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, suddenly, on a world saying “peace and security”. But believers are children of the day, so it will not catch them unprepared. They are to stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope, because God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through Jesus, who died for them.

Then a run of instructions for church life: respect those who lead and work hard among you; warn the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all; never repay evil; rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in everything; do not quench the Spirit, but test everything and keep what is good. The letter ends with a prayer that the God of peace will make them wholly holy, and a promise: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About times and dates there is no need to write, for they know that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying “peace and safety”, destruction will come on them suddenly, like labour pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape. But believers are not in darkness, so that day should not surprise them like a thief. They are all children of light and of the day. So let us not sleep like others, but stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God did not appoint us to suffer wrath but to receive salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that, awake or asleep, we may live with him. So encourage and build each other up, as you are doing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Destined for Wrath

God's purpose for his people was settled in advance, and settled on salvation rather than wrath (v.9) — not because of their performance but because the Lord Jesus ‘died for us’ (v.10), the only place in the letter where Paul states the substitution directly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Peace and security’ was close to an imperial slogan, and Paul names it as the moment of collapse.

Now: Paul tells them what they are — children of the day — before he tells them to stay awake (vv.5–6). Getting that order backwards is what produces exhausted Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, brothers and sisters, about times and dates we do not need to write to you, for you know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

The next question. Chapter 4 answered “What about our dead?” This answers “When?”, by politely declining.

Times and seasons. Chronoi, clock time, how long; kairoi, the decisive moment. Between them, every form of the question. Jesus used the same pair: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority” (Acts 1:7).

No need. In a few weeks Paul had given them not a schedule but a certainty and a posture.

The day of the Lord. The prophets’ phrase for God’s day of reckoning, “darkness, and not light” to those who complacently longed for it (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31). Paul gives God’s day to Jesus without explanation.

Like a thief. Jesus’ own image (Matthew 24:43; also 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 3:3). A thief is dangerous not because he is malicious but because he sends no word. So setting dates contradicts the teaching. Every generation that produced a timetable was refuted by this sentence before it began.

On a Tuesday. Ignore anyone who claims to know the date. Live today as if he might come.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While people are saying, “Peace and safety,” destruction will come on them suddenly, as labour pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

Peace and security. Eirēnē kai asphaleia: close to a Roman slogan. The pax Romana, peace and safety guaranteed by the legions, was on coins and inscriptions. Thessalonica, a free city that had backed Rome and prospered, believed the advertising. The prophets had heard it too: “saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14).

The moment of collapse. Not that the empire was uniquely wicked, but that a civilisation announcing its own permanence is the least prepared thing there is.

Labour pains. Sudden in onset, no one told the hour; but not unexpected, since she has known for months. Unpredictable in timing, entirely predictable in fact. And once it starts it cannot be called off.

A birth. Labour ends in birth. The New Testament uses birth-pain language for the end of the age because the pains precede something new (Matthew 24:8; Romans 8:22).

On a Tuesday. Distrust any security, national or personal, that does not include God.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order.

parallels.desc: Peace, peace, when there is no peace

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness, so that this day should surprise you like a thief. You are all children of the light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to the darkness.

But you. The paragraph turns from “them” to the church. Not that they avoid the day, but that it will not surprise them.

Lights on. A thief is a problem for a sleeping house. For a house with lights on and someone awake, his arrival is no catastrophe.

Children of light. A Hebrew idiom: “son of” means belonging to, characterised by (Luke 16:8; Ephesians 5:8). Not a target, but who they are.

All. Including the fainthearted and weak of v. 14.

You, then we. Paul cannot keep himself out: he is one of them.

The order. Not “stay awake and then you will be children of light”, but “you are, therefore stay awake”. Reverse it and you get exhausted Christians.

A textual note. A few important manuscripts read “like thieves”: the day will not catch you like thieves caught in the light. Most read “like a thief”, which fits v. 2.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, let us not be asleep like others, but let us stay alert and self-controlled. For those who sleep sleep at night, and those who get drunk get drunk at night.

A different sleep. In 4:13–15 “sleep” was a tender word for the Christian dead. Here, within a page, it is moral drowsiness. “Let us”: Paul includes himself.

Keep awake. The watchman’s word, and the disciples’ failure in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:40–41).

Be sober. Nēphō: clear-headed, able to see what is really there. Not solemnity (the letter commands joy in v. 16), but accurate judgement of what is temporary and what is permanent. Drunkenness is Scripture’s picture of the man who thinks he is fine and is not (1 Peter 5:8).

Night activities. In the ancient city, night was for sleeping and carousing (Romans 13:12–13). Believers do not belong to the night, so moral drowsiness is out of place, like a man asleep in the street at noon.

On a Tuesday. What dulls your spiritual alertness: screens, drink, busyness? Cut it back.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But since we belong to the day, let us be self-controlled, putting on faith and love as a breastplate, and the hope of salvation as a helmet.

How to stay awake. Not by trying harder to concentrate, but by getting dressed.

Isaiah’s armour. The LORD “put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head” (Isaiah 59:17). What God wears, he gives his people (Ephesians 6:13–17).

The triad returns. Faith, love and hope (1:3), first evidence of God’s work, now equipment for survival.

The placement. Faith and love over the heart: what keeps you alive. Hope over the head: what keeps you thinking straight. A church losing hope becomes unable to think clearly about the present, which is what happened when their friends died.

Defensive. No sword here. Not armed for a campaign but equipped to stay upright until the day.

On a Tuesday. When fear clouds your judgement, put on the helmet: remind yourself, in words, of the hope of salvation.

parallels.desc: righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God did not appoint us to suffer wrath but to receive salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

Appointed. God’s purpose, settled beforehand, settled not on wrath (compare 1:10). Not because of their performance.

To obtain. Acquisition, like an heir coming into an estate. Salvation is past, present and future; here, the future. They are not hoping to be spared; they are on their way to collect.

Who died for us. The only place in the letter where Paul states the substitution directly. Not because God overlooks things, but because someone stood where they stood (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Awake or asleep. The language of 4:13–18: alive or dead. Death changes nothing about the outcome (Romans 14:8).

Kept from the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians argue that because believers are not appointed to wrath, they cannot go through a future tribulation. But “wrath” here is God’s final judgment (1:10; Romans 5:9), not the trouble Christians suffer in this world, which they are “destined for” (3:3). Believers are kept from God’s wrath, not from all tribulation.

The real comfort. Not that they would be alive when he came; they all died. That it would not matter.

For worship. The wrath you deserved fell on him. Now nothing remains for you but life with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.

The second time. As at 4:18, a passage on the last day ends with “talk to each other”. Eschatology is given to be used on people who need it.

Build up. Oikodomeō, constructing a building course by course, behind our “edify”. Encouragement is structural work on another person, not general niceness.

One another. Ordinary members, before the leaders are even mentioned (v. 12).

As you are doing. The third such phrase (4:1, 10). Naming what is good and asking for more is harder than criticism, and more effective.

On a Tuesday. Text one believer today with a specific encouragement from Scripture.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Respect those who work hard among you, lead you in the Lord and warn you; hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work. Live in peace. Warn the idle, encourage the disheartened, help the weak, be patient with everyone. Make sure no one pays back wrong for wrong, but always strive to do good to each other and to everyone. Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus. Do not quench the Spirit or treat prophecies with contempt, but test everything; hold on to what is good, and reject every kind of evil.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment Instead of Either Extreme

Verses 19–22 refuse both easy positions: not contempt for what the Spirit gives, and not credulity, but testing — holding fast what is good and abstaining from what is bad. A church asked to be both open and awake has the harder, better task.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation only months old already had people labouring, leading and admonishing, honoured ‘because of their work’ (v.13).

Now: Verse 14 asks every member, not only leaders, to read the person in front of them: the idle need admonishing, the fainthearted encouraging, the weak holding up. And verse 18 asks for thanks in all circumstances, not for them.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ask you, brothers and sisters, to acknowledge those who work hard among you, who care for you in the Lord and who warn you. Hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work. Live in peace with each other.

One job, three sides. They labour (kopiaō, to weariness, as in 1:3); they are over you (proistēmi, to stand in front: leading and caring for); they admonish (noutheteō, correction meant to change). Probably the elders (Acts 14:23).

Months old. Already this church had people doing this. No titles; described by their work.

Respect. Literally “know”: recognise them, pay attention to who is actually doing the work.

Because of their work. Not office, gifts or personality. The honour is tied to something real.

What the work costs. Broken nights, the conversation nobody wants to have, the sermon written while the family waits. A church that sees this finds esteem easier (Hebrews 13:17).

Be at peace. Placed right after “esteem highly”: not so highly that you form parties around leaders (1 Corinthians 1:12).

On a Tuesday. Thank one of your church’s leaders this week for something specific they did.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We urge you, brothers and sisters: warn those who are idle and disruptive, encourage the disheartened, help the weak, and be patient with everyone.

Three people, three treatments. That is the point.

Admonish the idle. Ataktoi, a soldier out of rank: those who had stopped working, likely from excitement about Christ’s return (4:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:11). They need telling, not sympathy.

Encourage the fainthearted. Oligopsychoi, small-souled: courage run low, in a church burying friends. Tell a frightened person to pull himself together and you make him worse (Isaiah 35:3–4).

Help the weak. To take hold of, support, take someone’s arm. Not advice; bearing weight (Romans 15:1).

The wrong response does damage. The lazy man comforted stays lazy; the frightened man rebuked despairs; the weak man exhorted falls over. Read the person in front of you rather than giving what you find easiest. And Paul asks this of everyone.

Patient with all. Makrothymeō, long-tempered. All three will try you. Patience keeps you doing the right thing for the eleventh time.
verseByVerse.note: “Idle” may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s imminent return.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make sure that nobody pays back wrong for wrong, but always strive to do what is good for each other and for everyone else.

See that no one. The church is responsible for one another: retaliation is a community problem.

Who is told this. People with real grievances against identifiable neighbours, driven from families and trades. Not an ethic for the comfortable.

Beyond prohibition. “Pursue” the good of those making life hard. Jesus’ teaching: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27). The earliest churches received this ethic; they did not invent it (Romans 12:17–21).

What makes it possible. The Lord is an avenger (4:6), so the wronged need not secure justice themselves. And they are not destined for wrath (5:9): they received the treatment they are asked to extend.

What it does not mean. Not pretending the wrong did not happen, nor refusing to seek justice through proper authorities (Romans 13:4). It forbids personal revenge.

On a Tuesday. Do one good thing this week for the person who has wronged you.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

Impossible at first sight. Seven Greek words.

Rejoice always. Not “be cheerful about everything” to a grieving, persecuted church. Joy given by the Spirit in affliction (1:6). Possible always because its ground lies outside the circumstances (Philippians 4:4).

Pray without ceasing. Adialeiptōs was used of a persistent cough: recurring, never fully gone. Not uninterrupted formal prayer, which would make work impossible, but a line to God never closed: a heart turning to him through the day.

In, not for. Paul does not ask anyone to thank God for evil, a death or a betrayal. He asks for thanks to continue in such things, because God’s goodness does not pause.

God’s will. The second time the letter states it (4:3: sanctification). People agonise over finding God’s will. Two things at least are published: be holy, and rejoice, pray and give thanks.

Held together. Joy without prayer becomes shallow optimism; prayer without thanks, a list of complaints; thanks without joy, a duty.

On a Tuesday. Set three reminders on your phone today, each simply: “Thank you, Lord, for …”.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test them all. Hold on to what is good. Reject every kind of evil.

Quench. To put out a fire: the Spirit as flame (Acts 2:3). Fires are put out by smothering or by not feeding them.

Do not despise prophecies. Some evidently dismissed prophetic speech in the meeting. Soon a claimed message would say the day had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). When people have been misled by something claiming the Spirit, the instinct is to shut it all down.

Test everything. Neither credulity nor cynicism, but dokimazō, the assayer weighing metal (1 John 4:1; 1 Corinthians 14:29).

Two results. Hold fast the good; discernment that only rejects has failed half its job. And drop the bad entirely, whatever authority was claimed.

Does prophecy continue? At Thessalonica, before the New Testament was written, prophets spoke in the church and were to be weighed. Continuationist Christians believe such prophecy continues. The more likely view is that prophecy as new revelation belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20) and ceased when Scripture was complete. The principle remains: every claim to speak for God is tested by his written word.

Appearance of evil? The KJV’s “abstain from all appearance of evil” has been taken to mean avoiding whatever might look wrong. The word means form or kind: shun evil in every shape, not live by others’ impressions.

Open and awake. A church can be so afraid of disorder it quenches the Spirit, or so afraid of quenching him it swallows anything. Paul asks for the harder combination.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: May the God of peace himself make them holy in every way, and keep their whole spirit, soul and body blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus. The one who calls them is faithful, and he will do it. Pray for us. Greet all the believers with a holy kiss. Paul charges them before the Lord to have this letter read to all the believers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole Persons, and Who Does the Keeping

‘Spirit and soul and body’ (v.23) is a way of saying the whole of you, and they are to be kept — passive — by the God who calls them and is faithful (v.24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath of verse 27 ensured the letter reached every believer, the illiterate and the fainthearted included.

Now: The holy kiss for all the brothers (v.26) is a quiet demolition of rank: you cannot greet someone as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May God himself, the God of peace, make you holy through and through. May your whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

God himself. After all the commands (holiness, work, love, alertness, patience, testing), Paul prays, because no one produces this by effort.

Completely. Holoteleis, whole-to-the-end. Then said again: whole spirit, soul and body. Nothing left outside.

Three parts or two? Some read “trichotomy”: spirit, soul and body as three compartments. The historic Reformed view is “dichotomy”: spirit and soul name the one immaterial self from two angles. Scripture uses them in parallel (Luke 1:46–47), and the phrase works like “all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5), which no one takes as anatomy. It means the whole of you.

Be kept. Passive. They are not keeping themselves. That is the difference between exhaustion and rest (Jude 24).

Faithful. The guarantee is not their staying power but his character. He does not begin what he will not finish (Philippians 1:6).

Calls. Present tense, as at 2:12: he keeps calling.

For worship. “He will surely do it.” Rest your weight on that sentence tonight.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and sisters, pray for us. Greet all God’s people with a holy kiss. I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.

Pray for us. The apostle who prayed for them night and day asks for their prayers. The traffic runs both ways.

A holy kiss. The ordinary family greeting, extended to all: slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, rich and poor. You cannot greet someone as family every week and go on thinking him beneath you. “Holy” sets it apart from a merely social kiss (Romans 16:16).

Must we kiss? The command is for warm, sincere family greeting, in the form one’s culture uses. A handshake or embrace obeys it.

Under oath. Enorkizō, only here in Paul: strong. Letters were read aloud; most believers met Scripture with their ears. Paul wants no one left out: not the illiterate, the slaves who missed meetings, the fainthearted.

How the letter was regarded. Read to the whole assembly under oath. That is not how anyone treats private correspondence (compare Colossians 4:16).

A textual note. Some manuscripts add “also” (“pray also for us”), and many read “the holy brothers” in v. 27. Neither changes the sense.
verseByVerse.note: The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

The frame. Grace opened the letter (1:1) and closes it. A persecuted church, a congregation burying its dead, a slandered apostle and hard commands all sit inside grace.

To, then with. The greeting said “grace to you”, arriving. Here, “be with you”, staying. Paul could not come; he sends this.

What came next. More pressure, a second letter within months, and in time every one of them among those who had fallen asleep. The last word is what would still be true through all of it.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “Amen”.

For worship. The earliest surviving Christian letter ends, like all Paul’s letters, not with an exhortation but with grace, the provision that does not run out.
